newsitem.title: CHINA: China money supply close to target-central banker.
newsitem.headline: China money supply close to target-central banker.

text.p: The growth of China's money supply in 1996 largely met targets while the five major commercial banks wrote off 23.4 billion yuan ($2.8 billion) in bad debt, central bank governor Dai Xianglong said on Monday.

China's M1, or cash plus demand deposits of enterprises, grew by a year-on-year 18.9 percent in 1996 to more than 2.85 trillion yuan at the end of the year, said Dai, head of the People's Bank of China.
Broad M2 money supply grew by 25.3 percent year-on-year to more than 7.6 trillion yuan, he said in a speech at the opening of a five-day meeting of Chinese bankers in Beijing.

"Both of the two indices grew by rates very close to the targets we set at the beginning of 1996," the Xinhua news agency quoted Dai as saying. China's target for M1 growth was 18 percent and the goal for M2 was 25 percent.
China's M0, or cash in circulation, was up 11.6 percent to 91.7 billion yuan in 1996, compared with the 100 billion yuan limit imposed by the State Council, or cabinet, he said.
Deposits in China's banking system rose by 1.48 trillion yuan, or 27.5 percent last year, while loans increased by 1.06 trillion yuan, or 21 percent, he said.
Foreign exchange reserves expanded by $31.5 billion in 1996 to a record $105 billion at the end of December, he said.
China successfully employed monetary tools to fine tune the money supply, Dai said, adding that discount lending to state-owned commercial banks dropped by a net 61.6 billion yuan last year.
The central bank used 276.5 billion yuan to buy hard currency, he said without elaborating.
Discounted bills were valued at 354.5 billion yuan in January to November, he said.

China's five major commercial banks wrote off 23.4 billion yuan in dead and bad debts, he said. Officials have said they want to limit the amount used to write off bad debt in 1996 to no more than 30 billion yuan.
In 1997, China will continue to strictly follow a moderately tight monetary policy to curb inflation to a lower level than last year, he said.

China's benchmark retail price inflation was 6.0 percent last year, down from 14.48 percent in 1995, and well below the economic growth rate of 9.7 percent. Consumer price inflation last year was 8.3 percent.
